fact: SCPs are principal-centric AWS Organizations policies that cap identity-based and resource-based IAM permissions (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/iam-policy-types-how-and-when-to-use-them/)

The AgentCore Runtime execution role trust policy allows `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` to call `sts:AssumeRole` with `aws:SourceAccount` = your account and `aws:SourceArn` like `arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:<region>:<account>:*`, for confused-deputy protection (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)
Running an agent on AgentCore Runtime requires an execution role that trusts `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

The documented AgentCore Runtime execution role permissions cover six areas: `ecr:BatchGetImage` and `ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer` on the repository plus `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken`; CloudWatch Logs actions on `/aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/*`; `xray:PutTraceSegments`, `xray:PutTelemetryRecords`, `xray:GetSamplingRules` and `xray:GetSamplingTargets`; `cloudwatch:PutMetricData` limited to the `bedrock-agentcore` namespace; `bedrock-agentcore:GetWorkloadAccessToken*` on `workload-identity-directory/default/workload-identity/<agentName>-*`; and `bedrock:InvokeModel` and `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

Direct code deployment agents use a smaller execution role: the same as the container role without the ECR statements (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

`BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess` is the broad AWS managed policy for building on AgentCore and includes `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId`, which issues tokens for arbitrary user ID strings without IdP verification (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

For production, AWS advises copying only the needed statements from `BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess`, explicitly denying `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId`, and granting `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

AWS advises granting `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT` and denying `GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId` for production AgentCore agents (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

Auto-creating the AgentCore Runtime execution role from the console needs `iam:CreateRole` on `role/service-role/AmazonBedrockAgentCoreRuntimeDefaultServiceRole-*`, `iam:CreatePolicy` on `policy/service-role/AmazonBedrockAgentCoreRuntimeExecutionPolicy_*`, and `iam:AttachRolePolicy` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

The identity that runs `agentcore deploy` needs `sts:GetCallerIdentity`, access to the `CDKToolkit` and `AgentCore-<project>-<target>` stacks, CDK bootstrap or assume-role on the CDK roles, and permissions to create resources and pass roles (S3, ECR, CodeBuild, CloudWatch Logs, AgentCore) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)
AWS says to pre-bootstrap CDK and use least-privilege CDK roles in production for `agentcore deploy` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

`agentcore deploy` also tries to turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search, which needs `xray:UpdateTraceSegmentDestination` and `logs:PutResourcePolicy` among others; without those permissions the step is skipped (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

`agentcore config transactionSearch false` turns off the CloudWatch Transaction Search step of `agentcore deploy` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html)

Since 2025-10-13, for new agents the service-linked role `AWSServiceRoleForBedrockAgentCoreRuntimeIdentity` (principal `runtime-identity.bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com`) supplies AgentCore workload-identity permissions and replaces manual policies (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-oauth.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/service-linked-roles.html)

The AgentCore runtime identity service-linked role carries the policy `BedrockAgentCoreRuntimeIdentityServiceRolePolicy` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/service-linked-roles.html)

The identity deploying an AgentCore Runtime agent needs `iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole` for `AWSServiceRoleForBedrockAgentCoreRuntimeIdentity` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/service-linked-roles.html)

Other AWS managed policies for AgentCore are `BedrockAgentCoreNetworkServiceRolePolicy`, `AmazonBedrockAgentCoreMemoryBedrockModelInferenceExecutionRolePolicy`, `BedrockAgentCoreRuntimeInstancesServiceRolePolicy`, `BedrockAgentCoreRuntimeInstancesOperatorRolePolicy` and `BedrockAgentCoreRuntimeInstancesInstanceRolePolicy` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/security-iam-awsmanpol.html)

For custom or built-in-with-override strategies, AgentCore Memory needs a role passed in `memoryExecutionRoleArn` that trusts `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com`; memories without custom strategies ignore the role (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/long-term-configuring-custom-strategies.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore-readme.html)

The AgentCore Memory execution role can use `AmazonBedrockAgentCoreMemoryBedrockModelInferenceExecutionRolePolicy` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/long-term-configuring-custom-strategies.html)

The AgentCore Gateway service role is shared by all targets that use `GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE`, so its permissions are the upper bound for every caller; AWS advises minimal scope, separate gateways per trust boundary, and a policy engine on shared gateways (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-outbound-auth.html)

AgentCore Policy authorizes agent-to-tool calls through Gateway; Cedar policies are evaluated per tool call over a principal (for example `AgentCore::OAuthUser`), an action (`AgentCore::Action::"<Target>__<tool>"`), a resource (`AgentCore::Gateway`) and request context, with default deny and modes `ENFORCE` and `LOG_ONLY` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore-readme.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/awsforsap/aws-agentic-standard-operating-procedures-sops-for-erp-automation/)
AgentCore Policy policies are written in Cedar and the default decision is deny (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore-readme.html)
AgentCore Policy became GA in March 2026 after a preview from December 2025 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Managing AgentCore Policy engines and policies takes `bedrock-agentcore:CreatePolicyEngine`, `UpdatePolicyEngine`, `CreatePolicy`, `StartPolicyGeneration` and the related Get, List and Delete actions (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/secure-ai-agents-with-policy-in-amazon-bedrock-agentcore/)

Attaching AgentCore Policy to a gateway takes `bedrock-agentcore:UpdateGateway`, `ManageResourceScopedPolicy` and `ManageAdminPolicy` on the gateway (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/secure-ai-agents-with-policy-in-amazon-bedrock-agentcore/)

Cross-account AgentCore Runtime invocation needs two resource-based policies: `InvokeAgentRuntime` evaluates policies on both the agent runtime and the runtime endpoint, so both need an allow; OAuth-authenticated resources must use `"Principal": "*"` plus conditions such as `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-security-best-practices.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/resource-based-policies.html)
Cross-account AgentCore Runtime calls count against the resource owner's quotas (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)
AgentCore Runtime is invoked through the `InvokeAgentRuntime` API (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/resource-based-policies.html)

`put-resource-policy` on AgentCore replaces the whole policy, so multi-tenant updates must resend every statement (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/secure-multi-tenant-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-resource-based-policies/)

Since July 2026 an AgentCore Runtime can be restricted to accept calls only from your gateway: IAM runtimes use a resource-based policy with `aws:SourceArn`, and JWT runtimes use `allowedWorkloadConfiguration` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Runtime session context keys (October 2026) let sessions that share one execution role each be limited to their own data; this works on platform version V2 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

An SCP or IAM policy can force VPC-connected AgentCore deployments by denying `bedrock-agentcore:CreateAgentRuntime`, `UpdateAgentRuntime`, `CreateCodeInterpreter` and `CreateBrowser` when `bedrock-agentcore:subnets` or `bedrock-agentcore:securityGroups` is null (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/security-vpc-condition.html)

The AWS managed policies for Amazon Bedrock are `AmazonBedrockFullAccess`, `AmazonBedrockReadOnly`, `AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess`, `AmazonBedrockMarketplaceAccess`, `AmazonBedrockMantleFullAccess`, `AmazonBedrockMantleReadOnly` and `AmazonBedrockMantleInferenceAccess` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security-iam-awsmanpol.html)
`AmazonBedrockFullAccess` is one of the AWS managed policies for Amazon Bedrock (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security-iam-awsmanpol.html)

`AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess` lets Marketplace subscribe actions run only when called through Bedrock (`aws:CalledViaLast`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security-iam-awsmanpol.html)

Least-privilege Bedrock model access grants `bedrock:InvokeModel`, `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`, `Converse` and `ConverseStream` on specific `foundation-model` and `inference-profile` ARNs, for example `arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-*` plus `arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/us.anthropic.claude-*` (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/deploy-ai-agents-on-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-using-github-actions/)

For a geographic profile Bedrock authorizes the inference-profile resource, the source-Region model and each candidate destination-Region model; for a global profile it also authorizes the Region-agnostic `arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/...`, where `aws:RequestedRegion` is `unspecified` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html)

Region-deny SCPs must allow the cross-Region inference destination Regions or use the `bedrock:InferenceProfileArn` exemption (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html)
`aws-marketplace:Subscribe` can be limited to specific Bedrock models with the `aws-marketplace:ProductId` condition (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

A Bedrock model subscription made in one Region makes the model requestable in all Regions where it is offered, even if `Subscribe` is denied there (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

A custom Amazon Bedrock Agents (classic) service role needs model access, S3 read for OpenAPI action-group schemas, knowledge base query and optional guardrail, collaborator, Provisioned Throughput and KMS permissions (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-permissions.html)
Bedrock Agents (classic) action-group Lambda functions need a resource-based policy that allows Bedrock to invoke them (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-permissions.html)

Bedrock Knowledge Base builders need `bedrock:CreateKnowledgeBase`, `StartIngestionJob` and the related actions (or `AmazonBedrockFullAccess`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-prereq-permissions-general.html)

Managed Bedrock knowledge bases use a service role with model access, data-source access and an optional multimodal storage bucket, separate from builder permissions (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-managed-permissions.html)

SageMaker AI execution roles trust `sagemaker.amazonaws.com` and are passed with `iam:PassRole` on `CreateTrainingJob`, `CreateModel`, `CreateDomain`, `CreateProcessingJob` and similar calls (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-roles.html)
Passing a SageMaker AI execution role on create calls requires `iam:PassRole` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-roles.html)
`AmazonSageMakerFullAccess` is the broad managed policy option for SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-roles.html)

Lambda execution roles must trust `lambda.amazonaws.com`; Lambda assumes the role on invocation, and function code shouldn't call `sts:AssumeRole` on it (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-intro-execution-role.html)

When you create a state machine in the Step Functions console, it builds a least-privilege, Region-scoped role for Bedrock integrations (`InvokeModel`, `CreateModelCustomizationJob`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrock.html)
EventBridge rule target roles trust `events.amazonaws.com` (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/eventbridge-cross-account-targets)
EventBridge Scheduler roles trust `scheduler.amazonaws.com` and should carry confused-deputy conditions (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/troubleshoot-eventbridge-scheduler-errors)

On the client side, the IAM Identity Center administrator (management or delegated admin account) grants permission sets and assignments (secondary: inferred from the docs above) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/bedrock/latest/console/hp-guardrails-org-level-management.html)

src: aws organizations service control policy scp
fact: The Organizations management account owner controls SCPs, RCPs, AI opt-out policies and org-level Bedrock guardrail policies (secondary: inferred from the docs above) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/bedrock/latest/console/hp-guardrails-org-level-management.html)

The account administrator or IAM team grants execution roles, service-linked role creation and Marketplace subscribe rights (secondary: inferred from the docs above) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/bedrock/latest/console/hp-guardrails-org-level-management.html)

Marketplace private offers are accepted by the management account or a delegated admin (secondary: inferred from the docs above) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/managed-entitlements-subscribing.html)

Bedrock has PrivateLink interface endpoints including `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime` and Bedrock Mantle endpoints; endpoint policies can limit actions (for example `bedrock:InvokeModel`, `bedrock-mantle:CreateInference`) and principals (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-aws-privatelink-to-set-up-private-access-to-amazon-bedrock/)

IP-based conditions on Bedrock fail through VPC endpoints: `aws:SourceIp` isn't present when a request goes through a VPC endpoint, and network context is redacted when an AWS service calls Bedrock for you, so `IpAddress` conditions can't be met in those paths (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

AgentCore supports PrivateLink; the Gateway data plane endpoint is `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore.gateway` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/secure-ingress-connectivity-to-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-gateway-using-interface-vpc-endpoints/)

Control-plane PrivateLink for AgentCore Runtime, Memory, Gateway, built-in tools and Evaluations arrived in March 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
VPC egress for AgentCore Identity, Gateway and Runtime arrived in April 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

src: aws organizations resource control policy rcp
fact: RCPs cap what resources allow across the organization and are typically used for data perimeters with `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceVpc` and `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`; like SCPs, they don't apply to service-linked roles (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/building-a-data-perimeter-on-aws/perimeter-overview.html)
Bedrock stores customer content at rest in the Region where you use it, and prompts and outputs aren't shared with model providers (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/faqs/)

Bedrock geographic inference profiles keep processing within a geography (for example US, EU, APAC, Australia or Japan), while global profiles route to any supported commercial Region (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/securing-amazon-bedrock-cross-region-inference-geographic-and-global/)

An SCP can block Bedrock global inference profiles with `aws:RequestedRegion` `unspecified` plus `bedrock:InferenceProfileArn` like `arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/global.*` (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/securing-amazon-bedrock-cross-region-inference-geographic-and-global/ ; https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-service-unavailable-error)

Bedrock doesn't train models on customer data: AWS and third-party providers don't use Bedrock inputs or outputs to train Amazon Nova, Amazon Titan or third-party models, Bedrock doesn't store or review prompts and completions, and there's nothing to opt out of (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/amazon-bedrock-model-data-use ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ai/responsible-ai/nova-2-lite/overview.html)
Amazon Nova and Amazon Titan models on Bedrock aren't trained on Bedrock customer inputs or outputs (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/amazon-bedrock-model-data-use)
Amazon Titan models are offered on Bedrock and aren't trained on Bedrock customer data (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/amazon-bedrock-model-data-use)
Amazon Q Developer Free tier may use content for service improvement, while Q Developer Pro and Amazon Q Business don't (https://aws.amazon.com/q/developer/faqs/)

dst: aws organizations ai services opt-out policy
fact: You opt out of Amazon Q Developer content use with an AWS Organizations AI services opt-out policy for the console, Slack and Teams, and in IDE settings for the IDE (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_ai-opt-out.html)
Amazon Q Business doesn't use customer content for service improvement (https://aws.amazon.com/q/developer/faqs/)

AWS Quick says it doesn't train models on customer data; its stated attestations are HIPAA eligibility, FedRAMP, SOC 2 and ISO 27001 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-quick-aws-quick/)

The `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` condition key (added March 2025) works on `InvokeModel`, `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`, `Converse` and `ConverseStream`; an SCP with `Null` `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` = `true` denies calls that have no guardrail (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-permissions-id.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/implementing-least-privilege-access-for-amazon-bedrock/)

A specific Bedrock guardrail can be required by IAM or SCP through the `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` condition key (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-permissions-id.html)

A management-account Amazon Bedrock policy in AWS Organizations applies a guardrail to every model call in OUs or accounts, and an account-level default guardrail is also supported; when an application guardrail also applies, the union applies and the most restrictive control wins (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/bedrock/latest/console/hp-guardrails-org-level-management.html)

Org-level enforcement of a Standard-tier guardrail needs resource-based policies: both the guardrail and its guardrail profile (one per destination Region) must allow the organization, or calls fail with "The provided resource ARN is from a different account" (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-troubleshoot-guardrail-error)
AgentCore Policy supports Bedrock Guardrails (July 2026) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Bedrock model invocation logging is off by default; when turned on, it writes full requests, responses and metadata to CloudWatch Logs or S3 in the same account and Region for `Converse`, `ConverseStream`, `InvokeModel` and `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on `bedrock-runtime` only, and calls through `bedrock-mantle` aren't captured (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html)
Model invocation logging is a Bedrock setting that logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 in the same account and Region (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html)

In CloudTrail, Bedrock `InvokeModel`, `Converse` and their streaming variants are management events, while `InvokeAgent` (`AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias`), `Retrieve` and `RetrieveAndGenerate` (`AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase`), `InvokeFlow` and `ApplyGuardrail` are data events that need advanced event selectors (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html)

AgentCore Runtime data-plane calls `InvokeAgentRuntime`, `InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand`, `InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell` and `InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy` are CloudTrail data events with resource type `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime`; they aren't logged by default, and data events cost extra (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-session-endpoints.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/harness-operations.html)
AgentCore holds ISO and CSA STAR certifications (February 2026) and is in scope for SOC 1, 2 and 3 (July 2026) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AgentCore has been GA in AWS GovCloud (US-West) since May 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Bedrock is in scope for FedRAMP Moderate; SOC 1, 2 and 3 (since 2023-08-15); ISO 9001, 27001, 27017, 27018, 27701, 22301 and 20000; CSA STAR Level 2; and HIPAA eligibility and GDPR use (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/faqs/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/alps/security_bedrock/)

Bedrock inference is billed per token on demand, usually per 1M tokens; Priority tier costs 75% more than Standard, and Flex and Batch are 50% cheaper (as shown on 2026-11-14); the Reserved tier is set at account level through the AWS account team (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/)

Bedrock Provisioned Throughput is billed per model unit per hour (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-qwen-qwen3-coder-480b-a35b-instruct.html)

Bedrock Guardrails are billed per 1,000 text units: content filters and denied topics cost $0.15, sensitive-information filters and contextual grounding cost $0.10, Automated Reasoning costs $0.17 per policy, and regex and word filters are free (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/)

Managed Bedrock Knowledge Base index storage costs $5.00 per GB of raw data per month, Standard Retrieval $1.00 per 1,000 calls, and Agentic Retrieval $4.00 per 1,000 calls plus $1.00 per 1,000 underlying Retrieve calls (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/)

AgentCore Runtime microVMs V1 cost $0.0895 per vCPU-hour and $0.00945 per GB-hour, and V2 consumption costs $0.1276 per vCPU-hour and $0.0169 per GB-hour (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/)
AgentCore Gateway costs $0.005 per 1,000 invocations (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/)
AgentCore Identity costs $0.010 per 1,000 token or API-key requests, with no charge when used through Runtime or Gateway (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/)
AgentCore Policy costs $0.000025 per authorization request (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/)

AgentCore pricing is consumption based per component; observability is billed through CloudWatch and model calls are billed separately as Bedrock tokens (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/ ; https://repost.aws/articles/ARdXsMauGTTyCublA_hjzksw/domain-4-cost-management)

AWS Quick is billed per user per month plus a $250 infrastructure fee per account; users are billed at their highest tier in each period, prorated on upgrade (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/quick/pricing/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/quick/latest/userguide/monitoring-upgrades.html)
AWS Quick Essentials costs $3 per user per month with 1 agent hour (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/quick/pricing/)
AWS Quick Essentials includes 3 agent hours until 2027-01-31, then 1 agent hour (https://aws.amazon.com/quick/pricing/)
AWS Quick Professional costs $20 per user per month with up to 8 agent hours (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/quick/pricing/)
AWS Quick Enterprise costs $40 per user per month with up to 18 agent hours (as shown on 2026-11-14) (https://aws.amazon.com/quick/pricing/)

Amazon Q Developer Pro costs $19 per user per month (as shown on 2026-11-14); with an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, charges go to the payer account (https://aws.amazon.com/q/developer/pricing/ ; https://repost.aws/articles/ARgzzJODRETem1qD-NySaurw/implementing-a-cost-allocation-model-for-amazon-q-developer-subscriptions)
The Amazon Q Developer Free tier includes 50 agentic requests per month (https://aws.amazon.com/q/developer/pricing/)
Amazon Q Developer Pro needs an IAM Identity Center instance (https://repost.aws/articles/ARgzzJODRETem1qD-NySaurw/implementing-a-cost-allocation-model-for-amazon-q-developer-subscriptions)
SageMaker AI is pay-as-you-go with no AI-specific licensing; its pricing page wasn't checked for this note (unverified) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/)
Lambda is pay-as-you-go with no AI-specific licensing; its pricing page wasn't checked for this note (unverified) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/)
Step Functions is pay-as-you-go with no AI-specific licensing; its pricing page wasn't checked for this note (unverified) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/)
EventBridge is pay-as-you-go with no AI-specific licensing; its pricing page wasn't checked for this note (unverified) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/)

Bedrock inference is throttled on tokens per minute and requests per minute, per model and source Region; embedding models are throttled on RPM only, and defaults can be lower than published based on account age and history (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas.html)
`bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle` have separate Bedrock quota pools for the same model (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas.html)

Bedrock counts output tokens at a burndown rate against TPM: quota used = input + cache-write + output × rate, for example 5:1 for Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 4.5 and 1:1 for Claude Haiku 4.5 and Nova (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/run-generative-ai-inference-with-amazon-bedrock-in-asia-pacific-new-zealand/)
On Bedrock, Claude Opus 4.6 output tokens count 5:1 against TPM quota (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/run-generative-ai-inference-with-amazon-bedrock-in-asia-pacific-new-zealand/)
On Bedrock, Claude Haiku 4.5 output tokens count 1:1 against TPM quota (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/run-generative-ai-inference-with-amazon-bedrock-in-asia-pacific-new-zealand/)

Bedrock cross-Region quotas are separate: they appear as "Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute" per model in the source Region, and US geographic and global profiles draw from different pools (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/access-openai-gpt-models-on-amazon-bedrock-from-canada-with-cross-region-inference/)

AgentCore Runtime data-plane calls (`InvokeAgentRuntime` and the other data-plane APIs) share one adjustable quota of 1,000 TPS per account, and new sessions are limited to 25 TPS per account across all endpoints (consolidated in August 2026), replacing the 200 TPS per agent and 400 TPM per endpoint stated in the July 2026 notes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

`InvokeAgentRuntime` is an AgentCore Runtime data-plane API that counts against the shared 1,000 TPS per-account quota (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Runtime limits: active sessions 5,000 per account in us-east-1 and us-west-2 and 2,500 elsewhere (adjustable); 1,000 agents per account; synchronous request timeout 15 minutes; payload 100 MB; streaming duration 60 minutes; idle session timeout 15 minutes by default; maximum session 8 hours on microVMs and up to 14 days for async jobs on Instances (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Gateway default limits (adjustable): tool-call and tool-list rate 200 TPS per gateway and per account; 5,000 concurrent connections; search-based tool calls 25 TPM; payload 6 MB; 100 targets per gateway; invocation timeout 15 minutes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

Since August 2026 AgentCore Gateway owners can set their own rate limits scoped by JWT `sub`, IAM principal, target, tool or model, measured in RPS/RPM, TPM or connections; the effective rate is `min(service_managed, customer_configured)`, and `rate=0` blocks a caller (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Identity rate limits (all adjustable): `GetWorkloadAccessToken*`, `GetResourceOauth2Token` and `GetResourceApiKey` allow 200 TPS per account, `CompleteResourceTokenAuth` 100 TPS, and credential-provider CRUD 20 TPS; there are 50 OAuth2 and 50 API-key credential providers and 11,000 workload identities per account per Region (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Policy limits (not adjustable): 1,000 policy engines per account and Region with 1,000 policies each, a Cedar schema cap of 400 KB per engine, and `CreatePolicy` at 5 TPS (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

Lambda account concurrency defaults to 1,000 per Region and can be raised; throttled synchronous calls return HTTP 429 (secondary: AWS Compute Blog) (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/understanding-aws-lambda-scaling-and-throughput/)

AWS announced Amazon Bedrock AgentCore GA in October 2025 in nine Regions, with VPC support, 8-hour execution windows and session isolation (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-available/)
AgentCore has supported the A2A protocol since its GA in October 2025 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-available/)
AgentCore Gateway turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-available/)

As of 2026-11 the AgentCore devguide lists 13 modular services: Harness, Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity, Code Interpreter, Browser, Observability, Payments, Evaluations, Optimization, Policy and Registry, which work alone or together with any model (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html)

AgentCore services work with any framework, including CrewAI, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Strands Agents, Google ADK and OpenAI Agents SDK (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html)

The AgentCore harness (managed agent loop) has been GA since June 2026, with the What's New post dated 2026-06-17, after public preview started in April 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/06/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-harness-generally-available)

With the AgentCore harness you define a model, system prompt and tools in one config (`CreateHarness`) and call `InvokeHarness`; each session runs in an isolated microVM with filesystem and shell (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/06/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-harness-generally-available)
Since November 2026 the AgentCore harness defaults use Strands with Claude Opus 5 in commercial Regions (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
The harness is one of the AgentCore modular services, providing a managed agent loop (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/06/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-harness-generally-available)

AgentCore Runtime hosts agents or MCP servers in containers or direct code (serverless microVMs) and supports HTTP (port 8080 `/invocations`, `/ws`), MCP (port 8000 `/mcp`), A2A (port 9000 `/`) and AG-UI, with SigV4 or OAuth 2.0 inbound auth (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-service-contract.html)
AgentCore Runtime supports the AG-UI protocol alongside HTTP, MCP and A2A (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-service-contract.html)

An AgentCore Runtime "Instances" compute type with capacity providers was added in August 2026 and runs on EC2 in your account (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
Instances is an AgentCore Runtime compute type added in August 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Memory provides short-term and long-term memory, with episodic memory added in December 2025, TTL on long-term records in October 2026, and direct `IngestData` in August 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/12/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-policy-evaluations-preview/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AgentCore short-term memory moved to consumption-based pricing in October 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Identity is the agent identity and credential vault: it provides workload identities, OAuth2 and API-key credential providers for outbound calls, and token vault storage (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html)
AgentCore Identity works with Cognito, Okta, Entra ID and Auth0 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html)

AgentCore Identity additions include OBO token exchange (April 2026), Private Key JWT client auth (July 2026) and a Consent Portal (September 2026) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Policy in AgentCore has been GA since March 2026; policies sit in a policy engine attached to an AgentCore Gateway and are evaluated on every tool call (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/)
You author AgentCore policies in natural language that converts to Cedar (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/)
The AgentCore devguide now names the policy language Dogwood, which is Cedar-compatible (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html)

Bedrock Guardrails support was added to Policy in AgentCore in June 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html)
AgentCore Evaluations has been GA since 2026-03-31, in nine Regions at GA (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/agentcore-evaluations-generally-available/)

AgentCore Evaluations offers online evaluation of sampled production traces and on-demand evaluation for CI/CD, with 13 built-in evaluators plus custom LLM-judge or Lambda evaluators; Batch Evaluations and A/B Testing went GA in June 2026, and Failure Insights entered preview in June 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/agentcore-evaluations-generally-available/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Optimization (Recommendations, configuration bundles, A/B testing) has been GA since June 2026 after public preview from April 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Optimization optimizes system prompts and tool descriptions from traces, using A/B traffic splitting through Gateway (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Observability emits OTEL-compatible telemetry to CloudWatch, and cross-account monitoring was added in April 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AgentCore Observability telemetry is OTEL-compatible (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Since 2026-07-20, new AgentCore agents write spans to their own log group by default, while older agents keep `aws/spans` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Browser is a cloud Chrome runtime for Playwright and BrowserUse, with OS-level interaction since April 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Code Interpreter runs Python, JavaScript and TypeScript code sandboxes, with Node.js since March 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/what-is-bedrock-agentcore.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AgentCore Payments has been in preview since May 2026, with limited regional availability (secondary) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Payments handles x402 and Machine Payments Protocol microtransactions, with Coinbase CDP and Stripe (Privy) wallets (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AgentCore Payments supports Machine Payments Protocol microtransactions (preview since May 2026) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AWS Agent Registry (formerly "AgentCore Registry") has been GA since August 2026 after public preview from April 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AWS Agent Registry is a governed catalog of MCP servers, agents, skills and tools, with approval workflows, hybrid search and a native MCP endpoint (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
AWS Agent Registry reached AWS GovCloud (US-West) on 2026-11-06 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/aws-agent-registry-govcloud-us-west/)
Bedrock Agents is now "Bedrock Agents Classic" in maintenance mode (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)

Bedrock Agents Classic has been in maintenance mode and closed to new customers since 2026-07-30, gets no new features and has no planned end-of-life date (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)

AWS recommends migrating from Bedrock Agents Classic to the AgentCore harness, or to code-defined agents on AgentCore Runtime (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)
A migration skill for Bedrock Agents Classic is in the Agent Toolkit for AWS (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)

Bedrock Knowledge Bases are not affected by Agents Classic maintenance mode; in AgentCore you connect a knowledge base through AgentCore Gateway (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)

Bedrock Guardrails are not affected by Agents Classic maintenance mode: guardrails set on the model still apply, and agent-level enforcement in AgentCore goes through Gateway policies (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base (fully managed RAG) has been GA since June 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/06/amazon-bedrock-managed-knowledge-base/)

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base manages vector storage and offers hybrid search, reranking and agentic multi-hop retrieval, with six native connectors: S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive, OneDrive and Web Crawler (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/06/amazon-bedrock-managed-knowledge-base/)
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base integrates natively with AgentCore (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/06/amazon-bedrock-managed-knowledge-base/)

Bedrock Guardrails cross-account safeguards have been GA since April 2026: you enforce guardrails across an AWS Organization from the management account, at organization, account or application level (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/04/bedrock-guardrails-cross-account-safeguards/)

The Bedrock model catalog is serverless, and models are enabled by default (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/simplified-amazon-bedrock-model-access/)

Claude Opus 4.7 on Bedrock doesn't need the Anthropic first-time-use form (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-access.html)

Amazon SageMaker AI covers custom model training, fine-tuning and hosting; serverless model customization (SFT, DPO, RFT, LoRA, full fine-tuning) launched in December 2025 and expanded through October 2026, and training session APIs launched in October 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/12/new-serverless-model-customization-capability-amazon-sagemaker-ai/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/training-session-apis-on-sagemaker-ai/)

SageMaker AI serverless model customization and training session APIs run in us-east-1, us-west-2, ap-northeast-1 and eu-west-1, with training sessions also in ap-south-1 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/training-session-apis-on-sagemaker-ai/)

Lambda durable functions bring checkpointed multi-step workflows into Lambda with `steps` and `waits`, suspend for up to one year without compute charges, and support Python 3.13/3.14 and Node.js 22/24 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/12/lambda-durable-multi-step-applications-ai-workflows/)
Lambda durable functions launched in December 2025, initially GA in us-east-2 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/12/lambda-durable-multi-step-applications-ai-workflows/)

Step Functions has an optimized integration for the AgentCore harness with resource `arn:aws:states:::bedrockagentcore:invokeHarness` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrockagentcore.html)

AWS Quick (formerly Amazon Quick and Amazon Quick Suite, formerly QuickSight) is the business-user agent workspace, offering chat agents, autonomous and always-on agents, flows, apps and deep research (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-quick-aws-quick/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/09/amazon-quick-always-on-agents-sharper-feed-enterprise-controls/)
The rename from Amazon Quick to AWS Quick was announced in November 2026 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-quick-aws-quick/)
Quick Sight remains the BI component of AWS Quick (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-quick-aws-quick/)
Amazon Q Developer CLI and IDE became Kiro, and the Q Developer console became the Kiro console (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/upgrade-to-kiro.html)
In November 2026, Q Developer in the AWS Console was renamed "AWS assistant" (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/q-developer-renamed-aws-assistant/)
AWS MCP Server, AWS's managed remote MCP server, has been GA since 2026-05-06; its preview was announced at re:Invent 2025 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/05/aws-mcp-server/)
AWS MCP Server is part of the Agent Toolkit for AWS (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/05/aws-mcp-server/)

One AWS MCP Server endpoint lets an agent call any AWS API, run sandboxed Python, search and read docs, and load agent skills, with IAM guardrails, CloudWatch metrics and CloudTrail logging, at no additional charge (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/05/aws-mcp-server/)
AWS MCP Server endpoints follow the pattern `https://aws-mcp.<region>.api.aws/mcp` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

The AWS MCP Server setup guide lists us-east-1, us-west-2, ap-southeast-1, ap-southeast-2, ap-northeast-1, eu-central-1, eu-west-1 and eu-west-2, newer than the May 2026 GA post, which listed only us-east-1 and eu-central-1 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

AWS MCP Server has about a dozen tools in two groups: no-credential tools (search and read documentation, list Regions, regional availability) and IAM-authenticated tools (`aws___call_aws` for any API, run script in a sandbox, retrieve skill, get tasks, S3 presigned URL) (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/how-amazon-cloudfront-secures-and-accelerates-the-aws-mcp-server/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/understanding-iam-for-managed-aws-mcp-servers/)

AWS MCP Server auth option A is OAuth 2.1 through AWS Sign-in with no local proxy; access tokens last 1 hour and auto-refresh for up to 12 hours, and multi-profile switching is not supported (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

For AWS MCP Server OAuth, the principal needs the managed policy `AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy` (`signin:AuthorizeOAuth2Access`, `signin:CreateOAuth2Token`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

Some clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, Kiro IDE) need `?oauth=initialize` appended to the AWS MCP Server URL (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

`aws signin create-oauth2-token-with-iam --grant-type client_credentials` is the headless client-credentials path for AWS MCP Server OAuth: it signs with SigV4 and returns a Bearer token that lasts 3600 s (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/introducing-oauth-support-for-aws-mcp-server/)
The AWS MCP Server OAuth support announcement is dated 2026-07-09 (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/introducing-oauth-support-for-aws-mcp-server/)

AWS MCP Server auth option B is SigV4 through the MCP Proxy for AWS: run `uvx mcp-proxy-for-aws-cli@latest https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp --metadata AWS_REGION=us-west-2`, which needs AWS CLI ≥ 2.32.0 and uv; this option supports read-only mode, multiple profiles and a default Region (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

Claude Code adds AWS MCP Server for OAuth with `claude mcp add aws-mcp https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp --transport http` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

MCP Proxy for AWS (`mcp-proxy-for-aws`, PyPI) is GA, open source and at version 1.8.0 (2026-11-03); GA was announced in October 2025 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/model-context-protocol-proxy-available/ ; https://pypi.org/pypi/mcp-proxy-for-aws/json)

MCP Proxy for AWS SigV4-signs MCP traffic to AWS-hosted MCP servers and to AgentCore Gateway or Runtime endpoints, and has read-only mode and retries (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/model-context-protocol-proxy-available/)

IAM context keys `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` (bool) and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` (string, for example `aws-mcp.amazonaws.com`, `eks-mcp.amazonaws.com`, `ecs-mcp.amazonaws.com`) cover all AWS-managed MCP servers and can be used in IAM policies or SCPs to deny or limit actions an agent takes through MCP, for example to deny S3 deletes through MCP (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/understanding-iam-for-managed-aws-mcp-servers/)

The boolean IAM context key `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` is set on calls made through AWS-managed MCP servers such as AWS MCP Server (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/understanding-iam-for-managed-aws-mcp-servers/)
AWS Knowledge MCP Server (remote, no AWS account, rate-limited) has been GA since October 2025 (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/aws-knowledge-mcp-server-generally-available/)

AWS Knowledge MCP Server's endpoint is `https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws` with no auth, and its tools are `search_documentation`, `read_documentation`, `recommend`, `list_regions` and `get_regional_availability` (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/aws-knowledge-mcp-server-generally-available/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/accelerate-region-expansion-with-the-aws-knowledge-mcp-server/)

AWS now recommends the AWS MCP Server instead of the AWS Knowledge MCP Server (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/accelerate-region-expansion-with-the-aws-knowledge-mcp-server/)

The AWS setup guide says to remove `aws-api-mcp-server` and `aws-knowledge-mcp-server` when you adopt AWS MCP Server, because overlapping tools confuse agents (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)

The awslabs/mcp README calls the Agent Toolkit for AWS the successor for production (https://github.com/awslabs/mcp)

The deprecated awslabs Amazon Kendra Index MCP Server is replaced by AWS MCP Server (https://github.com/awslabs/mcp)

AgentCore Gateway aggregates MCP targets into a single virtual MCP server with one `tools/list`; target types are Lambda functions, API Gateway REST API stages, OpenAPI schemas, Smithy models, remote MCP servers, built-in integration templates and built-in connectors (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-targets-mcp.html)
AgentCore Gateway offers semantic tool search and target-level 3LO OAuth, which went GA in April 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-targets-mcp.html)

Since June 2026 AgentCore Gateway has HTTP passthrough targets and inference targets that route LLM traffic to providers through model-based routing, and AgentCore Runtime targets went GA in June 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-supported-targets.html)

October 2026 added a Step Functions connector, MCP Tasks, model fallback and private CA for targets to AgentCore Gateway (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Gateway built-in integration templates cover 16 providers: Amazon, Asana, BambooHR, Brave, Coinbase x402 Bazaar, Confluence, Jira, Microsoft, PagerDuty, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Slack, Smartsheet, Tavily, Zendesk and Zoom (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-target-integrations.html)
The AgentCore Gateway built-in Web Search Tool connector went GA in June 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
The AgentCore Gateway built-in Web Answer connector went GA in November 2026 in us-east-1 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Gateway inbound auth options are JWT (`CUSTOM_JWT` with `discoveryUrl`, `allowedAudience`, `allowedClients`, `allowedScopes` and `customClaims`), IAM (`AWS_IAM`, which needs `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway`) or offloaded ("Authenticate only" and `NONE`) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-inbound-auth.html)

The AgentCore CLI defaults gateway inbound auth to `NONE` (unauthenticated) if you omit `--authorizer-type` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-using-auth-ex-starter.html)
AgentCore Gateway outbound auth to targets uses the IAM role, API keys or OAuth through AgentCore Identity (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-inbound-auth.html)

The AgentCore Gateway URL pattern is `https://{gateway-Id}.gateway.bedrock-agentcore.{Region}.amazonaws.com`, the control plane is `bedrock-agentcore-control.<region>.amazonaws.com`, and the service principal is `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

`bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com` is the recommended Bedrock inference endpoint and serves InvokeModel, Converse, OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses (at `/openai/v1`), and the Anthropic Messages API (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)

`bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws` serves Responses, Chat Completions and Messages; both Bedrock endpoints run on the same Mantle engine at the same per-token price (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)
`bedrock-runtime` serves the OpenAI-compatible Responses and Chat Completions APIs at `/openai/v1` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)
`bedrock-runtime` serves the Anthropic Messages API, and `bedrock-mantle` serves Messages too (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)

Only `bedrock-runtime` supports Guardrails, intelligent prompt routing, custom inference profiles, batch and Provisioned Throughput (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)

Only `bedrock-mantle` supports server-side tools (such as web search), background inference (`background=true`), Projects and Workspaces (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)
Mantle inference IAM uses `bedrock-mantle:CreateInference` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/scaling-throughput-best-practices.html)

Bedrock API keys (bearer tokens) work with the OpenAI SDK: set `OPENAI_BASE_URL` to the Bedrock base URL and `OPENAI_API_KEY` to the Bedrock key (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/api-keys.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-responses-api.html)

Short-term Bedrock API keys last up to 12 hours, inherit the caller's IAM permissions and are recommended by AWS; long-term keys create an IAM user with `AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess` and are meant for exploration only (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/api-keys.html)
A long-term Bedrock API key creates an IAM user with `AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/api-keys.html)
boto3, the Python package for AWS calls, is at version 1.44.3 (https://pypi.org/pypi/bedrock-agentcore/json)
Strands Agents, the open-source agent framework, is at version 1.65.0 (https://pypi.org/pypi/bedrock-agentcore/json)

`bedrock-agentcore`, the AgentCore runtime SDK for Python (`BedrockAgentCoreApp`), is at version 1.26.0 (2026-11-10) (https://pypi.org/pypi/bedrock-agentcore/json ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agentcore-python-sdk-reference.html)

There is also an AgentCore client in the AWS SDK for Python v4 docs, installed with `pip install aws-sdk-bedrock-agentcore` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-python/v4/reference/clients/bedrock-agentcore/)
JS/TS agent work on AWS uses the `@aws-sdk/*` v3 clients (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agentcore-python-sdk-reference.html)

A2A and AG-UI are supported agent protocols on AgentCore Runtime; the `ProtocolConfiguration.serverProtocol` values are `MCP | HTTP | A2A | AGUI` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_ProtocolConfiguration.html)
AgentCore Runtime accepts `AGUI` as a `ProtocolConfiguration.serverProtocol` value (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_ProtocolConfiguration.html)
The AgentCore Runtime protocol port is configurable from 8000 to 12000, except 8443 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_ProtocolConfiguration.html)

AWS Quick is an MCP client for external MCP servers, supporting SSE and streamable HTTP with 3LO, 2LO or no auth, and discovers OAuth through RFC 9728 and Dynamic Client Registration (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/quick/latest/userguide/mcp-integration.html)
Since August 2026 AWS Quick can enable MCP servers and agents from AWS Agent Registry (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/08/aws-agent-registry-agents-mcp-servers-quick/)

AWS Quick has built-in action connectors to SaaS; thirteen were added in April 2026, including Google Workspace apps, Zoom, QuickBooks, Airtable and Dropbox, alongside the earlier Salesforce, Jira, ServiceNow and Microsoft 365 connectors (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/04/amazon-quick-google-workspace-zoom/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/09/amazon-quick-custom-apps-natural-language/)

The common event-driven agent pattern is EventBridge (rules or Scheduler) to Lambda to `InvokeAgentRuntime`; AWS samples trigger AgentCore Runtime agents from schedules and webhooks this way (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/building-a-context-aware-ai-assistant-on-agentcore-and-openclaw/)

In the event-driven agent pattern, a Lambda function calls `InvokeAgentRuntime` to run an AgentCore Runtime agent (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/building-a-context-aware-ai-assistant-on-agentcore-and-openclaw/)

PrivateLink interface endpoints for Bedrock use the suffixes `bedrock`, `bedrock-runtime`, `bedrock-mantle`, `bedrock-agent` and `bedrock-agent-runtime`, each as `com.amazonaws.<region>.<suffix>` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html)

PrivateLink has three interface endpoints for AgentCore: `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore` (data plane), `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore-control` and `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore.gateway` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html)
AgentCore VPC endpoint policies can only filter IAM principals, so OAuth callers need `Principal: *` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html)

JDBC and ODBC drivers don't apply to the in-scope AWS agent services (IAM, Bedrock, AgentCore, Lambda, Step Functions, EventBridge), which are reached through HTTPS APIs and SDKs; database drivers belong to separate database services (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)
AWS CLI v2 is at 2.40.3, tagged 2026-11-13, with its changelog on GitHub (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/aws-cli/v2/CHANGELOG.rst ; https://api.github.com/repos/aws/aws-cli/commits/2.40.3)

On Windows, install AWS CLI v2 with the signed PowerShell script `irm https://awscli.amazonaws.com/v2/install.ps1 | iex` (recommended; per user to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Amazon\AWSCLIV2`, `-System` for all users) or the MSIs `msiexec.exe /i https://awscli.amazonaws.com/AWSCLIV2.msi` (all users) and `AWSCLIV2-User.msi` (current user) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html)

On Linux and macOS, install AWS CLI v2 with `curl -fsSL https://awscli.amazonaws.com/v2/install.sh | bash`, adding `--system` for all users (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html)

A winget package `Amazon.AWSCLI` exists in the winget-pkgs repo (newest manifest 2.40.2), but AWS install docs do not list winget (secondary) (https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs/tree/master/manifests/a/Amazon/AWSCLI)

`aws login` signs the CLI in with console credentials and is the recommended local-dev method; it works for root, IAM users and federated identities, `--remote` handles devices without a browser, and credentials auto-refresh every 15 minutes for up to the principal's session limit (max 12 h) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sign-in.html)

The `aws login` cache is `%USERPROFILE%\.aws\login\cache` (override with `AWS_LOGIN_CACHE_DIRECTORY`), the profile gets `login_session = <arn>`, and `aws logout [--all]` signs out (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sign-in.html)

You can restrict `aws login` with IAM by targeting `arn:aws:signin:region:account-id:oauth2/public-client/localhost` (same device) and `.../remote` (cross-device); for SDKs that don't support login credentials yet, serve them through `credential_process` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sign-in.html)

`aws configure sso` and `aws configure sso-session` set up IAM Identity Center sign-in by writing an `[sso-session]` section with `sso_start_url`, `sso_region` and `sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access`, plus a profile with `sso_account_id` and `sso_role_name` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-files.html)
After configuring SSO you run `aws sso login [--profile X | --sso-session Y]`, and tokens are cached in `~/.aws/sso/cache` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html)

PKCE has been the default `aws sso login` flow since CLI 2.22.0 and must complete on the same device; use `--use-device-code` for headless devices (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/developer/aws-cli-adds-pkce-based-authorization-for-sso/)

The AgentCore CLI is installed with `npm install -g @aws/agentcore` and is at v1.0.3 (Node ≥ 20.12.0); v1.0 shipped in October 2026, after GA as v0.4.0 in March 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agentcore-get-started-cli.html ; https://registry.npmjs.org/@aws/agentcore/latest ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

Key AgentCore CLI commands are `agentcore create`, `add gateway`, `add gateway-target`, `add credentials`, `deploy`, `invoke`, `migrate` (v0 projects) and `update` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agentcore-get-started-cli.html)

On Windows, the old pip `agentcore` command can shadow the npm one; if `agentcore --version` errors, run `pip uninstall bedrock-agentcore-starter-toolkit` and open a new terminal (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agentcore-get-started-cli.html)
Kiro CLI (`kiro-cli`, formerly Amazon Q Developer CLI) is AWS's agentic coding CLI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/upgrade-to-kiro.html)

Kiro CLI version 2.11 and later can add AWS MCP Server natively with `kiro-cli mcp add --name aws-mcp --url https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)
The Agent Toolkit for AWS ships agent skills installed with `npx skills add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/skills` (https://aws.amazon.com/products/developer-tools/agent-toolkit-for-aws/)
AWS recommends pinning the MCP proxy version, for example `mcp-proxy-for-aws@1.6.3`, for reproducible behavior (https://aws.amazon.com/products/developer-tools/agent-toolkit-for-aws/)

The hashicorp/aws Terraform provider v6.73.0 (2026-11-11) has AgentCore resources including `aws_bedrockagentcore_gateway`, `aws_bedrockagentcore_gateway_target`, `aws_bedrockagentcore_agent_runtime` and `aws_bedrockagentcore_memory` (https://api.github.com/repos/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/releases/latest ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/main/website/docs/r/bedrockagentcore_gateway.html.markdown)
The hashicorp/aws Terraform provider is at v6.73.0 (2026-11-11) (https://api.github.com/repos/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/releases/latest)

AWS CDK AgentCore constructs graduated to stable in May 2026, but the Policy submodule is still alpha; the AgentCore CLI now generates a thin CDK app on `@aws/agentcore-cdk` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)
CloudFormation and Pulumi `aws-native` expose `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::*` resources (https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/aws-native/api-docs/bedrockagentcore/gatewayrule/)
Pulumi `aws-native` exposes `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::*` resources such as the gateway rule (https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/aws-native/api-docs/bedrockagentcore/gatewayrule/)

The Agent Toolkit for AWS docs (AWS MCP Server setup, quotas, OAuth) are at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/ (verified 200), and the repo is https://github.com/aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html)
awslabs MCP docs are at https://awslabs.github.io/mcp/ (verified 200), with source at https://github.com/awslabs/mcp (https://awslabs.github.io/mcp/)
AWS Knowledge MCP is a docs MCP server at `https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws` (verified 200) (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/aws-knowledge-mcp-server-generally-available/)
The documentation tools in AWS MCP Server need no credentials (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/aws-knowledge-mcp-server-generally-available/)

Bedrock `bedrock-runtime` throttling is per model and per Region (TPM, sometimes also RPM), and all APIs share the quota: InvokeModel, Converse, Responses and Chat Completions, even though quota names say "InvokeModel" (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-runtime.html)
`bedrock-mantle` quotas are counted separately from `bedrock-runtime`, with separate input and output TPM and no RPM (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html)

Bedrock output tokens burn down quota faster than input tokens: for recent Claude models each output token counts as 5, and quota use = input + cache-write input + output × burndown rate (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/global-cross-region-inference-for-latest-anthropic-claude-opus-sonnet-and-haiku-models-on-amazon-bedrock-in-thailand-malaysia-singapore-indonesia-and-taiwan/)

An unset `max_tokens` is a top cause of agent throttling: Bedrock reserves input + `max_tokens` at admission, and if `max_tokens` is unset it reserves the model maximum (for example 64,000 for Claude Sonnet); the unused part is returned after completion (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/optimize-your-applications-for-scale-and-reliability-on-amazon-bedrock/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html)

Cross-Region inference (CRIS) profiles raise throughput, and each profile type has its own quota pool; geographic profiles use prefixes such as `us.` and `eu.`, global profiles use `global.`, and quotas such as "Global cross-Region model inference tokens per minute for ${Model}" are viewed and raised in the source Region (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/access-openai-gpt-models-on-amazon-bedrock-from-canada-with-cross-region-inference/)

Cross-Region inference fails with `AccessDeniedException` when SCPs block destination Regions: geographic CRIS needs every destination Region allowed, global CRIS needs `aws:RequestedRegion` = `unspecified` and the Region-agnostic ARN `arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/...`, or you can exempt with the `bedrock:InferenceProfileArn` condition key (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html ; https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-access-denied-exception)

On `bedrock-runtime`, the Responses API rejects `background=true` (400) and application inference profiles (400) and has no server-side tools; stored responses belong to the Region that served them (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html)

A wrong `bedrock-mantle` path prefix makes requests fail: some models are served under `/v1` and others under `/openai/v1`, and a wrong prefix returns "model ... isn't supported on this route" (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-responses-api.html)
Listing models against the `bedrock-runtime` `/openai/v1` URL returns `404 UnknownOperationException` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-chat-completions.html)

AgentCore Runtime session limits: synchronous request timeout 15 min, async jobs up to 8 h on microVMs (14 days on Instances), payloads capped at 100 MB, streaming connections up to 60 min, idle timeout default 15 min (`idleRuntimeSessionTimeout`), max session lifetime default 8 h (`maxLifetime`), and 1 GB session storage (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Runtime throttles at 1,000 TPS for data-plane calls and 25 TPS for new sessions, both adjustable and shared per account, simplified in August 2026 from 200 TPS and per-endpoint limits; control-plane mutations are 50 TPS (not adjustable), active sessions are 5,000 in us-east-1 and us-west-2 and 2,500 in other Regions, and cross-account calls count against the owner's quota (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html)

AgentCore Runtime images are capped at 2 GB on platform V1 and 10 GB on V2; direct-code zips are 250 MB compressed and 750 MB uncompressed; environment variables are 4 KB per agent; sessions get 2 vCPU/8 GB by default, up to 8 vCPU/32 GB with resource configurations on V2 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Gateway limits (all adjustable): 100 targets per gateway, 1,000 tools per target, 15 min invocation timeout, 6 MB tool payloads, tool-call and tool-list rates of 200 TPS per gateway and per account, 5,000 concurrent connections, 25 search-based tool calls per minute, and 10 TPS each for Web Search and Web Answer (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Memory limits: 150 resources per Region, 200 `CreateEvent` per second per account, 5 per second per actor and session, and 150,000 TPM for long-term extraction (adjustable) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)
AgentCore Browser allows 1,000 concurrent sessions, each with 1 vCPU/4 GB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)
AgentCore Code Interpreter allows 1,000 concurrent sessions, each with 2 vCPU/8 GB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

AgentCore Policy has a 400 KB Cedar schema cap per policy engine that grows with tool count and parameter complexity across all attached gateways, so split engines if you hit it; Policy APIs run at 1 to 5 TPS (not adjustable) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html)

A Gateway-to-Runtime auth mismatch fails with "Authorization method mismatch": an IAM runtime needs an IAM (SigV4) or Caller-IAM target, and a JWT runtime needs an OAuth or token-passthrough target (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-resolve-authorization-method)

AWS MCP Server rate limits are not adjustable: authenticated requests get 10 per second sustained per account per Region, unauthenticated requests get 5 per second per source IP and only the read-only knowledge tools, and throttled requests return 429 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/aws-mcp-limits.html)

Lambda limits for agent tools: timeout 900 s (90 min for Managed Instances async and ESM invocations); synchronous payloads 6 MB each way, async payloads 1 MB, streamed responses up to 200 MB at 2 MBps after the first 6 MB; default concurrency 1,000 per Region, with new accounts starting lower (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html)

STS `AssumeRole` `DurationSeconds` goes up to 43,200 s (12 h), subject to the role's max session setting, but role chaining caps sessions at 1 hour and any value above 3,600 s fails when chaining (https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/iam-role-chaining-limit)

Agent identity blueprints support inheritable permissions: an admin grants a permission once on the blueprint principal and every agent identity from that blueprint inherits it (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/agent-blueprint).
"Required resource access" on a blueprint is only a declaration and grants nothing (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/agent-blueprint).

A Foundry resource's public network access flag can be Disabled (private endpoint only, target sub-resource labelled "account"), "Enabled from selected IP addresses", or All networks; DNS uses a `privatelink` subdomain zone, and only Approved private endpoints carry traffic (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/configure-private-link).

Foundry Agent Service outbound isolation injects the agent client into a customer subnet delegated to `Microsoft.App/environments` (size /27 or larger) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/configure-private-link).

The AI gateway in Foundry is an Azure API Management instance created from the Foundry portal (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/configure-private-link).

The EU data zone for DataZone deployment types uses the EU Data Boundary, which may include EFTA countries such as Norway and Switzerland (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/deployment-types).

Global deployment types such as `GlobalStandard` may process prompts in any region, while data at rest stays in the customer geography (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/deployment-types).

Foundry guardrails (previously content filters) are named collections of controls covering Hate, Sexual, Self-harm, Violence, user prompt attacks, indirect attacks, protected material (text and code), PII (preview), Task Adherence (preview), Groundedness (preview, models only) and Spotlighting (preview, models only) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/guardrails/guardrails-overview).

The OpenAI-compatible v1 endpoint is `https://<resource-name>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/` and works with the standard OpenAI SDKs (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/sdk-overview)
The Azure OpenAI v1 endpoint accepts either API keys or Entra tokens with scope `https://ai.azure.com/.default` (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/sdk-overview)
The Azure OpenAI v1 endpoint accepts Microsoft Entra tokens for `https://ai.azure.com/.default` (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/sdk-overview)
